title: What should you ask first in a profitability case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a profitability case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first whether the whole industry's profits are falling or only the client's, then split profit into revenue and costs before you guess at a cause. The trap is diagnosing too early: naming a culprit before you have split revenue by product, region or channel and seen which part actually moved.
body:
The first question to ask

Is the whole industry seeing this, or just us?

The answer halves your search. If every competitor's margin fell, look outside: input prices, a demand shift, regulation. If only the client is suffering, look inside: its prices, its mix, its costs, its channels. Pair it with two quick facts: the profit figures over time (how much, since when) and what the client wants (back to the old margin, or a target).

How to build your structure

  • Revenue: units × price, then split by product, customer segment and channel.
  • Costs: fixed versus variable, each line compared with last year and with competitors.

Then quantify before you explain. Find which branch moved by the most money, and spend your time there. The full tree, with every branch, is in the profitability framework.

A miniature profit bridge

A delivery restaurant made $500k of revenue last year and $50k of profit, so costs were $450k. This year revenue is $520k but profit is $20k, so costs are $500k. Costs rose $50k while revenue rose only $20k: that is the $30k fall. Margin went from 10% to 3.8%.

Split the $50k. Delivery-platform commissions rose $35k and packaging rose $15k; everything else held steady. So this is not a demand problem. The next question is why commissions rose: more orders, worse terms, or a shift from direct orders to the platform?

Suppose the average order is $20 in both years (25,000 orders last year, 26,000 this year) and the platform takes 25%, or $5 an order. A $35k rise in commission means 7,000 more orders went through the platform. With only 1,000 more orders in total, about 6,000 orders moved from direct to the platform. Each one now earns $5 less. The fix is about channel, not menu prices or marketing spend.

The trap most people fall into

Diagnosing before splitting. Candidates hear "profits fell" and jump to "costs must be up" or "we should raise prices" without checking which product, region or channel moved.

Weak: "Profits are down, so I'd look at cutting costs and maybe raising prices."
Strong: "Revenue grew 4% but costs grew 11%, and 70% of the cost rise is platform commission. Before any fix, I'd like to know whether orders shifted from our own channel to the platform."

The strong version names the size of each piece and asks for the one fact that decides the next step.

Two prompts to try

A grocer's operating margin fell from 4% to 2% in two years, while sales grew.

Show the answer
  • Prices and mix: discounting to match rivals; a shift to lower-margin categories.
  • Cost of goods: supplier prices, shrinkage and waste; share of private label.
  • Store costs: wages, energy, rent, per store and as a % of sales.
  • Online and delivery: online share of sales; cost to pick and deliver each order.

Where to start: sales grew but margin halved, so find which cost grew faster than sales, measured as a % of sales.

The trap: talking about growing sales when the problem is margin.

A casual-dining chain's profit per restaurant has halved in three years.

Show the answer
  • Covers: guests per restaurant per week; lunch versus dinner, weekday versus weekend.
  • Spend per guest: menu prices, drinks, desserts; discounts and vouchers.
  • Food and drink costs: ingredient prices and waste; menu mix towards low-margin dishes.
  • Restaurant costs: staff hours and wages; rent, energy, delivery fees.

Where to start: covers. Rent and staff are largely fixed, so a small fall in guests cuts profit hard (see operating leverage).

The trap: blaming food inflation without checking whether fewer people come in.
